keyAndScale.modalCharacter: Mixolydian-influenced Major - the bVII (F chord) adds punk grit to the major key
keyAndScale.relativeMinor: B minor is the relative minor of D major

mainProgression.description: About as simple as rock gets - a two-chord verse progression that is the backbone of punk rock. The alternation between D and G creates a bouncing, infectious rhythm.

sectionProgressions.description: Guitar riff establishing the bouncy D-G alternation that drives the entire song
Simple two-chord alternation with driving downstrokes, the definition of punk simplicity
The chorus introduces the F major (bVII) borrowed from Mixolydian mode, giving the 'should I stay or should I go' hook its distinctive tension
The 'this indecision's bugging me' bridge section built on the same chord vocabulary

harmonicFunction: D (I) - Bright, confident major tonic establishing the punk rock energy
G (IV) - Subdominant creating the bouncing back-and-forth with the tonic
F (bVII) - Borrowed chord from Mixolydian mode adding gritty punk tension in the chorus

techniques.name: Punk Downstroke Strumming
techniques.description: Fast, aggressive all-downstroke strumming on open chords and power chords that defines the punk rock rhythm guitar approach

notes: D: X-X-0-2-3-2 (open D major) or D5: X-5-7-7-X-X (power chord)
G: 3-2-0-0-3-3 (open G major) or G5: 3-5-5-X-X-X (power chord)
F: 1-3-3-2-1-1 (barre chord) or F5: 1-3-3-X-X-X (power chord)
All-downstroke eighth notes for the authentic punk feel
Mix of open chords and power chords depending on the section
sequence: Start with the open D chord, strumming steady eighth-note downstrokes
Transition to G with a quick hand shift while maintaining rhythm
In the chorus, move to the F barre chord (or F5 power chord)
Keep the right hand moving in constant downstroke motion
Accent beats 1 and 3 slightly for the driving pulse
tips: All downstrokes are essential for the punk attack - resist the urge to alternate pick
Keep the strumming hand loose at the wrist to avoid fatigue
The D to G transition should be instant - practice until there's no gap
If the F barre chord is too difficult, use an F5 power chord (1-3-3-X-X-X)
details.progression: D - G (verse) / D - G - F - G - D (chorus)

techniques.name: Call-and-Response Guitar Riff
techniques.description: The signature answering guitar riff played between vocal phrases, using double stops and hammer-ons that give the song its distinctive character

notes: Double stops on the B and high E strings (2nd and 1st strings)
Hammer-on from open to 2nd fret on the G string
The riff answers the vocal line in a classic call-and-response pattern
Based on D major pentatonic shapes in open position
sequence: Play the D chord and strum the pattern
During the vocal gap, play the answering double-stop riff
Hammer-on from open G string to 2nd fret for the signature sound
Return to strumming for the next vocal phrase
tips: Listen to the recording to get the exact timing of the fills
Keep the fills simple and rhythmic rather than flashy
The fills should complement the vocal melody, not compete with it
Practice switching between strumming and the fill seamlessly
details.progression: Fills between D and G chord strumming

techniques.name: Barre Chord Basics (F Chord)
techniques.description: Introduction to the F barre chord shape as it appears in the chorus, a gateway barre chord skill for beginners

notes: F: 1-3-3-2-1-1 (full barre chord at 1st fret)
F5: 1-3-3-X-X-X (power chord alternative)
The F chord is one of the first barre chords most guitarists learn
In this context, it only appears briefly in the chorus, making it manageable
sequence: Place index finger across all strings at the 1st fret
Add remaining fingers for the E-shape barre chord
Practice pressing firmly and strumming to ensure all strings ring
Drill the transition from G to F and F back to G
If the full barre is too hard, use F5 power chord instead
tips: Roll your index finger slightly so the harder edge presses the strings
Place your thumb behind the neck, directly behind the 1st fret
You only need the F chord briefly in the chorus - don't let it stop you from playing the song
The F5 power chord is a perfectly valid substitute for beginners
details.progression: G - F - G transition in the chorus

sections.name: Intro
sections.description: The bouncy guitar intro establishing the D-G alternation with Mick Jones' characteristic scratchy tone
notes: Open D and G chords with aggressive downstroke eighth notes
Set the tempo and energy for the entire song from bar one
The scratchy, slightly overdriven tone is part of the character
Count in: the intro establishes 114 BPM before the vocal enters

sections.name: Verse
sections.description: Driving two-chord verse with the simple D-G alternation supporting the iconic vocal melody and call-and-response guitar fills
notes: Keep the strumming driving and consistent throughout
The simplicity is the point - don't try to make it more complex
Small guitar fills answer the vocal between phrases
Maintain the punk energy without overpowering the vocal

sections.name: Chorus
sections.description: The anthemic the signature chorus introducing the F chord for that gritty Mixolydian flavor
notes: The F chord arrival is the harmonic surprise of the chorus
Hit the F chord with extra emphasis for maximum impact
Quick G chord between F and D acts as a passing turnaround
The progression resolves back to D with a satisfying landing

sections.name: Bridge
sections.description: The the iconic vocal hooks bugging me' bridge with more emphasis on the guitar fills and the G-F-G movement
notes: The bridge starts on G rather than D for a different harmonic perspective
Lead guitar riff becomes more prominent in this section
Energy builds through the bridge toward the final chorus
The Spanish-language backing vocals add distinctive texture

sections.name: Outro
sections.description: Extended chorus repetition building to the chaotic punk rock ending with increasing intensity and energy
notes: Maximum punk rock intensity for the outro repetitions
Strumming becomes more aggressive and loose
The whole band pushes the energy to its peak
Final resolution on a ringing open D major chord

alternatives: Any guitar with a single bridge pickup
guitar.pickup: Bridge pickup for punchy, cutting punk tone

alternatives: Any amp pushed into natural breakup

effects.distortion: Natural amp overdrive - no pedals needed for authentic Clash tone
effects.reverb: Minimal or none - dry punk sound
effects.other: No effects necessary. The raw, direct guitar-to-amp tone is essential for punk authenticity.

beginner.focus: Learn the two-chord verse and basic strumming - this is a perfect first rock song
steps: Master the open D and G chord shapes
Practice transitioning between D and G smoothly
Learn the all-downstroke eighth-note strumming pattern
Play along with the verse sections of the recording

intermediate.focus: Add the F chord for the chorus and play the complete song
steps: Learn the F barre chord (or F5 power chord substitute)
Practice the chorus transition: D - G - F - G - D
Play through the entire song structure at 114 BPM
Add the call-and-response guitar fills between vocal phrases
intermediate.timeEstimate: 2-3 weeks for complete song with fills

advanced.focus: Add dynamics, authentic punk attitude, and perform with full energy
steps: Perfect the call-and-response riff with exact timing
Add dynamic contrast and authentic punk strumming aggression
Practice singing while playing the rhythm part
Work on stamina for the all-downstroke approach at tempo

commonMistakes: Using alternate picking instead of all downstrokes - downstrokes give the punk attack
Making the song too complex - the beauty is in the simplicity
Rushing the tempo - lock in at 114 BPM, not faster
Over-distorting the tone - The Clash used crunchy overdrive, not heavy metal gain
practiceRoutine: Warm up with D and G chord transitions at relaxed tempo for 3 minutes
Practice all-downstroke eighth notes on D chord at 100 BPM for 3 minutes
Run through the verse (D-G) pattern at increasing tempos for 5 minutes
Add the chorus (D-G-F-G-D) progression for 5 minutes
Play through the complete song once at 114 BPM
focusAreas: Clean, instant D to G chord transitions
Smooth integration of the F chord in the chorus
Punk attitude and energy throughout the performance
metronomeWork: Start at 80 BPM with D-G chord changes on steady downstrokes
Increase by 10 BPM per session until reaching 114 BPM
Practice the chorus chord sequence with metronome on beats 2 and 4
Target: play the entire song at 114 BPM with no dropped beats
